title: Sandokai Part 3
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing both our individual uniqueness and our interconnectedness with others. It suggests that we should find a sense of harmony by recognizing how each person has their own unique role or "show" in life, while also acknowledging our connection to the larger community. By reconciling these two aspects, we can cultivate a deeper understanding of ourselves and our place in the world, ultimately finding unity and balance in our daily lives.

sentences.text: This sutra is on page 10 in the sutra books, [unclear: "because I won't have thought about it"].
I especially love this sutra for its striking imagery and the images that challenge conventional thinking, such as, in light there is darkness, in darkness there is light.
Light and dark are like the front and back foot in walking.
Ooh, that's an interesting image.
A phenomenon exists like a box and lid fitting together perfectly.
Principle accords with phenomena like arrow points meeting in midair.
Very exciting image.
I find all of these images describe things that are either really hard to imagine, or require absolutely perfect conditions to occur at all.
And perfection is part of what this sutra is about.
As Tim told us in our first talk, the sutra is about the Buddha mind being transmitted to us down through the ages and available to all of us no matter where we're from.
Then John talked about the second part of the sutra: reality is made up of two kinds of things, the obvious, palpable, discernible stuff and the non-obvious.
And those two are intertwined.
The title says merging of difference and unity, so that's what the sutra is about.
Like John, I used the translation and the commentary about the sutra by [unclear: "Shukaku of living by bow"].
So I will be reading a few passages from that tonight.
But first, because we haven't chanted this for a while, I thought we could just do that together.
It's on page 10.
*Merging of difference and unity.
The mind of the great sage of India is intimately transmitted from west to east.
While human cavities are [unclear: "sharp to call"], the way has no norther and southern ancestors.
The spiritual source shines clear in light.
The branching streams roll on to the dark.
Grasping at things is surely a delusion.
According to the same, this is still not enlightenment.
All the objects of the senses interact and yet do not. [unclear: "Inracting words is involvement"].
Otherwise, speech keeps its place. [unclear: "Sites vary in quality and form"].
Sounds differ as squeezing or harsh.
Refined and common speech come together in the dark.*
*Clear and murky phrases are distinguished in light.
The four elements return to their natures just as a child turns to his mother.
Fire beats, wind moves, water wets, [unclear: "breathes solid"], eye and sight, hearing sounds, nose and smells, tongue and taste.
Thus, we reach everything depending on these roots. [unclear: "We reach that fourth.
Trumpet branches share justice, revering on each other's speech"].
In the light there is darkness, but don't take it as darkness.
In the dark there is light, but don't see it as light.
Light and dark oppose one another like the front and back foot in walking.
Each and every thing has its merit, expressed according to function and place.
Phenomenon exists, box and lid fit.
Principle responds, arrow points meet.*
*Hearing the words, understand the meaning.
Don't set up standards of your own.
If you don't understand the way of life before you, how will you know the path as you walk?
Progress is not a matter of power or measure, but if you are confused, comments and words lock your way.
I respectfully urge you to study history, do not bash your days and nights in vain.*
So, starting with the lines "dark and light oppose one another," and I'm taking this from a slightly different translation, I see, I'll read this part.
*In the light there is darkness, but don't take it as darkness.
In the dark there is light, but don't take it as light.*
When I read that, I get confounded by the double negatives that happen there: there's light, but don't take it as dark, but don't take it as that.
I get confused and confounded.
Well, Okumura is using a different translation and his is a little easier for me at least to understand.
He says:
*Right in light there is darkness, but don't confront it as darkness.
Right in darkness there is light, but don't see it as light.*
So it's a little easier for me to deal with that wording.

Light means, and this is a confusing part too for the way I think about things, relative truth in this sutra: the dualistic world of words and thinking by which we discriminate things one from another.
And darkness means absolute truth, unavailable to our conscious thinking, but universally true, like the concept of no self or big self and little self, that kind of thing.
The use of the words light and darkness in this way is a bit counterintuitive, to me at least.
Usually we associate light with enlightenment in western civilization, with truth, and we associate darkness with obscurity or maybe untruth.
So associating light with the dualistic view and dark with the truth of absolute unity takes a little effort on our part.

But what the sutra means is that darkness prevents us from distinguishing one thing from another as our dualistic minds do, and in that way it helps us realize and remember the universal emptiness of all things: the truth that phenomena have no abiding permanent characteristics.
Everything is always changing.

And the word light permits us to discriminate among things, to think dualistically, which we also need to do to live in the world, even though we must realize also that this type of thinking does not get us to universal truth.
In this section, the sutra is saying that light and darkness are interpenetrating each other.
Moreover, both are necessary for us to understand the nature of truth.
So we should not try to separate them out from each other.
We should understand that light and dark are always together.
There is darkness in light and light in darkness, or in other words, absolute truth always exists within conventional understanding, and conventional and relative truth exists within universal truth.
Phenomena and experience, or experiences both absolute and relative, not one or the other.
Quoting:
*Light and darkness are always together.
We cannot understand our life through only one aspect.
Darkness, unity, or non-discrimination are enlightenment, and discrimination is delusion.
From this perspective, enlightenment means to give up light, or differentiation and discrimination, and to live in the realm of non-discrimination.
In the phrase light and dark, light refers to samsara, and dark to nirvana, or non-discrimination.
But these are inseparable aspects of reality.
In Mahayana Buddhism, our practice is not to escape samsara or nirvana.*
Nirvana is within samsara, samsara being the endless round of birth, suffering, and death.
Nirvana is within samsara, which is within nirvana.
We cannot make this life all nirvana or all samsara, because samsara and nirvana always exist together.
Right in samsara, there is nirvana.
It's a pretty sophisticated, heady concept, but a good teaching.
The next lines: light and dark oppose one another like front and back foot in walking.
Our chant book translation uses "oppose," which I usually interpret as one foot trying to stop or prevent the other foot from moving.
But that's a naive impression.
Here "oppose" actually means opposite, just opposite, not conflicting.
And both elements in the opposition are necessary for the unified outcome of walking, or realizing reality or truth.
Okumura's translation makes this more obvious.
He says, light and dark are relative to one another, like forward and backward steps.
That's a little easier for me to get with.
Like dark and absolute and light and relative, the front and back foot are a pair of opposites that create a unity or oneness, walking.
Just as light and darkness are opposites that equally create oneness, the front foot and the back foot each equally contribute to the oneness of walking.
The sutra continues:
*Light and dark are relative to one another like forward and backward steps.
There is no light without darkness and no darkness without light.
But what do forward and backward steps mean?
In walking, when the right foot is forward, the left foot is backward.
When the right foot is backward, the left foot is forward.
In this sense, light and darkness are like right and left feet.
They are always together.*
*But sometimes we see only light and sometimes only darkness.
Sometimes darkness is forward, sometimes light.
But light and darkness are always together, just like our feet when we are walking.*
So that really helped me to understand that image and connect it with the idea.

And I remember many, many years ago my first teacher, [unclear: "Govincino"], once said to us, well, if all the electricity left and there were no more lights in the world, we would still shine because we have energy.
So we would shine.
And that was really such an encouraging thought, that in fact we don't need artificial light.
Life itself shines.
So I think about that kind of light being in darkness and darkness in light.
Okumura has much more to say about light and dark and front and back feet and their double meanings.
If you're interested, I encourage you to read this book, because it's quite a complex thing that he's trying to explain here.
For now though, we'll move on to the last section of the sutra to be discussed.
It reads:
*Each of the myriad things has its merit expressed according to function and place.
Phenomena exist like box and lid joining, principal accords like arrow points meeting.*
Or as the translation that Okumura uses, a little bit different:
*All things have their function.
It is a matter of use in the appropriate situation.
Phenomena exist like box and cover joining, principal accords like arrow points meeting.*
Essentially this section of the sutra is saying that everything is as it should be.
Each thing has its function and place in the world, including us.
Each thing has integrity or suchness just as it is.
And it expresses its suchness in the way it functions or the place it occupies.
Phenomena or forms exist perfectly just as they are, like a lid fitting perfectly to its box.
The lid must be just right for the box, otherwise neither can function as they are meant to do.
The perfectly fitting lid has integrity and permits the box to have integrity.
I used to make pottery many, many years ago and one of the challenging projects was to make a pot with a cover that fit it.
The difficulty with doing that is the pottery shrinks as it dries and as it gets fired.
So you have to predict how much it's going to shrink and so forth, and how fit the walls are.
It's quite a challenge.
Getting it to fit just perfectly is pretty rare, and I made lots of lids that didn't fit.
So whenever there was one that really fit well, it was a real thrill to have done that, and it didn't come from my skill, more from good luck at that point.
All things have their function.
Everything and everybody has a unique function.
We all have different capabilities, talents, characteristics, personalities, bodies and languages.
All things have a function appropriate to some situation.
Isn't that great?
That's so reassuring.
When we get up in the morning and say, I wonder what I'm doing.
The word in Japanese for appropriate situation is show, meaning place.
S-H-O.
Each of us has to find the best place to use this body and mind.
This unique body and mind exists as an intersection of difference and unity.
That is the place where we can create our own unique way of life.
That is our practice.
Our practice doesn't mean we have to make ourselves into a particular shape.
We are not like cars with certain standard shapes and qualities.
We have a responsibility to accept this unique body and mind and put it to use.
To fulfill the potential of this body and mind we have to find an appropriate situation and embrace it as our own life, as our own work.
Hallelujah.
Regarding the words phenomena and principle in these two lines, Okumura says that phenomena refers to particular things or beings and principle refers to the unity or universality of all beings.
Thus phenomena and principle work together, completely joined, inseparable.
The wonderful image of arrow points meeting emphasizes the perfection of all phenomena and experience just as they are.
The meeting arrow points is a reference to a classic Chinese story about two expert archers, a master and his best student.
The student challenges the master to a duel with their bows to prove that his skill is now superior to the master's.
The two aim and shoot at each other and their arrows are so perfectly shot that they hit head on in midair.
It's so great.
He really is a great student and the master must have been very proud of him.
The sutra says that phenomena and principle, difference and unity, should meet just like arrows.
Our practice is to actualize this relationship between difference and unity in each situation.
For example, we cannot live by ourselves.
We are part of a community and yet no matter where I live, I am I.
I cannot be another person, and yet to be a member of a community, I have to transcend "I am I" and see the situation of the whole community.
We have a point of view as an individual and also as a member of the sangha or community.
We also have another I who sees the situation from both perspectives.
The viewpoint of an individual person is in this case an example of difference.
It's very natural that I have an opinion different from that of other people.
We shouldn't negate our individual opinions, but as a member of a community we have to see things as a whole.
The most desirable condition is when both ways of seeing meet each other like arrows shot by the masters.
If we can perceive a situation like that, we can be really peaceful.
It doesn't happen very often because it's really difficult.
Our way of life is like arrows missing each other.
That's why we have pain in our social lives.
There is no way another person or a god can make arrows meet.
Our practice is to find the appropriate situation in which this person as an individual and this person as a member of the sangha can meet like a box and lid joining or like two arrows in midair.
Beautiful description of sangha life.
So this part of the sutra is saying in these lines, one, that reality is both obvious and non-obvious and that our practice is to discover and work with both levels or kinds of truth.
Two, that both kinds of truth are in all phenomena and that our practice is to hold both and not to focus on just one kind.
And three, that all phenomena, everything, has legitimacy, has its proper place and function in the world.
Everything, including each of us, is meant to be just what we are individually as well as to be part of the larger whole.
And our practice is to negotiate this paradox of being both me and us.
*May our intentions equally extend to everything.
With the true and meritorious way, beings are [unclear: "possible to passable"].*
